svg.text: A stretch response unfolds across overlapping feedback loops
As time passes, feedback can incorporate broader anatomy, more of the task, and voluntary strategy.
An unexpected load stretches the flexor
The mechanical event initiates several feedback processes.
Same perturbation, different instructions; traces and intervals are schematic.
One perturbation enters loops with different latency and reach
Early feedback is dominated by local spinal circuitry; later feedback can recruit other joints, goals, and broader networks.
Rapid feedback protects the shared goal
A shared task can recruit both limbs rather than restore one joint in isolation.
The perturbation changes limb mechanics and initiates
Approximate upper-limb intervals; boundaries depend on muscle, perturbation, background activation, and preparation.
alpha motor axons: final common path for this muscle
Later feedback is not a slower copy of the first response; it can recruit a broader solution to the task.
The unperturbed limb responds within the long-latency interval,
shaped to preserve tray orientation rather than mirror the local response.
The useful distinction is not reflex versus voluntary control: anatomical reach and task sensitivity expand over time.
Each recruited muscle is reached through its motor neurons, but the task determines which motor pools participate.
